evidence.paraphrase: Kīrti asks how the Śakti-born Dhundhirāja can stand with a foot at Tuṇḍana while holding the demon in Vārāṇasī. Gṛtsamada answers through the Lord’s unlimited cosmic form: feet through seven nether regions, head in heaven, hands/feet/eyes/ears everywhere, universes in the hair pores, beyond gods’ and sages’ complete knowledge. Even nectar and poison can exchange effects by his will. He urges abandoning doubt and hearing the sin-removing account. This is the source’s theological answer, not a modern geographical identification.

evidence.verification_notes: Author witness-level Sanskrit reading checked; independent Sanskrit expert/printed-edition verification pending.

evidence.paraphrase: Solar-lineage Divodāsa is learned, generous, honored, self-controlled, helpful and free of desire for others’ property. Pleased by his tapas, Brahmā gives the excellent kingdom of drought-stricken Kāśī; the king accepts under the exclusion of all gods. He performs the functions of Sun, Indra, Fire, Wind and Moon, and his tapas brings rain. His wife is faithful, charitable and obedient; the digital naming phrase is unresolved. He uses learned advisers for conduct, law and penance rather than royal punishment. Gods follow Śiva to Mandara mountain; no premature death, grief or calamities afflict the kingdom, crops flourish and offerings return. Gods and king praise one another.

evidence.paraphrase: Kīrti asks why Śiva and the gods left Vārāṇasī. After twelve years of drought and loss of offerings, gods following Brahmā’s advice ask Śiva to visit Mārīci, who has practiced ten thousand YEARS at Mandara. Śiva goes with gods and finds him nearly skeletal, about to die without that visit. Pleased by the tapas, he gives his own form and sends him by vehicle to his own realm with attendants and music. Śiva remains on the mountain. Seeing no fault in Divodāsa, he sends gods to inspect; each finds none, installs a liṅga by his own name and stays in Kāśī.

evidence.paraphrase: All social orders and āśramas follow their duties; students serve gurus, wives observe fidelity, charity and vows, ascetics practice silence and bathing, and householders perform eight stated rites. Rain/crops prosper, without barren or bereaved households or pests. The king requires sight of Viśveśvara, Mādhava, Dhundhi, Bhairava, Daṇḍapāṇi, Guha and Gaṅgā, bathing at Maṇikarṇī and honoring Bhavānī before eating. Śiva cannot take a faultless kingdom. He sends eight Bhairavas to induce a slight wrong, then Ādityas,64Yoginīs, Durgā, dikpālas, sages and remaining gods. None finds a fault; they stay, establish liṅgas or practice tapas. Durgā remains outside town and fulfills people’s desires. Śiva laments that only Dhundhi and Mādhava have not been sent.

evidence.paraphrase: Śiva hymns Dhundhi as cosmic cause, Pradhāna/Puruṣa, divider of guṇa functions and chosen divine offspring. Distressed by Kāśī’s separation, he takes refuge. Dhundhi asks why the all-knowing Śiva sent only others. Śiva asks him to go to Avimukta and use māyā to delude people so Divodāsa’s merit declines. Dhundhi promises to accomplish the purpose and remove the ruler who shares the people’s sin. He bows to Śiva, Pārvatī, Ṣaḍānana and Nārada as guru, circumambulates and leaves. Finding only merit in Kāśī, he immediately assumes an astrologer’s role.

evidence.paraphrase: The astrologer appears golden and beautiful, with divine ornaments and yellow clothing. An embedded parenthesis adds32marks and knowledge of past/present/future. Faithful women desire and follow him, leaving families to ask questions. He answers thoughts, interprets dreams he has shown through māyā, gives effective boons: leprosy disappears and infertile women have children. He reads past/future acts from hands, identifies hidden objects and tells an unprompted poor questioner he will be wealthy in three days, which happens. People marvel and give wealth and gems.

evidence.paraphrase: After two or three months the news reaches the court. Royal wives seek him without the husband’s permission; friends arrange secret visits. They wash and anoint his feet/body, offer betel, ask questions and become absorbed in him, abandoning household tasks and hiding visits when the king rises. Divodāsa invites and worships him, offers cow, arghya, wealth and clothing, asks privately and forgets his former deity. He offers villages, grain and money to keep him close. The astrologer says he left family and possessions and wants no wealth; his payment is obedience to a visitor arriving on the seventeenth day, which will benefit the king. No actual arrival date is restated in47.

evidence.paraphrase: The king swears to obey the astrologer. People in Kāśī abandon their duties and serve him. Viṣṇu assumes the explicitly named Bauddha role outside the five-krośa boundary, creating delusion through māyā. His source-attributed teachings criticize embodied worship, ritual offerings and gifts, stress enjoyment of one’s body and the dissolution of elements at death; the narrator calls them contrary to śruti/smṛti. His wife Kamalā similarly persuades women using non-difference of selves in different bodies. The text reports abandoned fidelity, offerings, charity and ritual conduct and increased wrong. These are this narrative’s strategies and judgments, not a historical description of Buddhist teaching.

evidence.paraphrase: The Bauddha visitor is honored by Divodāsa. He says Kāśī was made and sustained by Śiva, righteous residents seek liberation, Bhairava expels sinners, and the king’s residence depended on merit now declining. Divodāsa agrees, remembers the astrologer’s prediction and asks who has come for his welfare. Viṣṇu reveals four arms, conch, discus and mace, then collective/individual consciousness forms. The king calls himself and his parents blessed, says Brahmā forcibly gave the kingdom after his earlier renunciation/tapas, and takes refuge seeking freedom from birth/death. Viṣṇu promises supreme liberation through Viśveśvara and directs renunciation. After reflection the king recognizes the astrologer as Gaṇeśa and the Bauddha as Hari. Viṣṇu reveals four arms with lotus as well; the king offers the royal seal and asks liberation, saying Śiva should rule his own land. Viṣṇu says Śiva will grant it.

evidence.paraphrase: Viṣṇu returns to his Bauddha āśrama and sends a messenger to Śiva, reporting increased wrong through his strategy and the kingdom abandoned with the astrologer’s help. He asks Śiva to return to Vārāṇasī. Divodāsa gives up royal insignia, installs a liṅga in his own name in a fine temple and undertakes tapas while awaiting Śiva. The liṅga is described as liberation-giving and fulfilling desireful worshippers’ wishes. Printed26 is absent in the revelation passage, although the body and terminal42 are intact.

evidence.paraphrase: Dhundhi resumes his own form after the king’s renunciation, remains a giver of desires and sends his own return message. Śiva joyfully rides his bull back with attendants/music, favors fasting Jaigīṣavya and bows to Dhundhi. His hymn attributes creation, preservation and destruction to the deity’s guṇa division, cosmic powers and devotees’ grace. It recalls Prakṛti worshipping him before overcoming Mahiṣa, and Śeṣa supporting earth through devotion. These are attributed precedents, not newly read full battles. Śiva rejoices in regained Avimukta.

evidence.paraphrase: Śiva asks Dhundhi always to guard his devotees and Kāśī. He says residence requires the grace of Dhundhi, Bhairava and Daṇḍapāṇi before he gives liberating Brahman at death. He requests removal of distress and wishes/wealth for worship at moonrise on a Tuesday Māgha fourth, with cakes/modakas and the hymn. Reading the hymn at morning or three twilights, or once, gives enjoyment/liberation; the Dhundhi name removes sins and its remembrance accomplishes tasks. These are Śiva’s stated petitions and phalas, not a separately quoted Gaṇeśa acceptance. He installs a Gaṇḍakī-stone Dhundhi image and temple, returns home with the gods, and actually grants his devotee Divodāsa liberation. Gṛtsamada explicitly says Viṣṇu’s māyā brought the king’s welfare.

evidence.paraphrase: After Gṛtsamada finishes the Dhundhi account, he receives permission and returns to his āśrama. Kīrti takes her son to Dhundhi’s shrine at Vārāṇasī on a Tuesday Māgha fourth. The festival’s wealth, food, ornaments and offerings obscure the divine face. Thinking herself poor and unable to match these gifts, she offers dūrvā, śamī and Mandāra gathered on the road and asks her son’s advancement. The Lord values their devotion more than wealth. Others leave; mother and son remain fasting. Dhundhirāja appears from the image with ten arms, crown, yellow clothing, tusk and jewels. They are overwhelmed and forget even worship/bowing. He invites a boon and declares the leaves/flowers more pleasing than riches.

evidence.paraphrase: Kīrti regains bodily awareness and reluctantly speaks because the all-knowing Lord directs her. Her hymn praises cosmic transcendence and all forms, and calls her eyes, birth, husband, son, parents, lineage, knowledge and tapas blessed. She recalls divine naming, poison death and Gṛtsamada’s revival through devotion. She requests devotion for her son, outstanding three-world fame, detachment in rule, long life, virtues, strength, renown, happiness, patience, victory in every battle and love for brāhmaṇas and gods.

evidence.paraphrase: After receiving the boons, Kīrti spends the remaining night, bathes and worships at dawn, then leaves with her son, happy yet grieving separation. Both chant Dhundhi’s name. The king’s procession, army and music bring them to Karṇapura, decorated with flags, sprinkling and incense. He smells and embraces his son’s head, addresses Kṣipraprasādana affectionately, gives gifts and hears Kīrti’s full report; the couple reunite. After some days, recognizing the son’s virtues and policy knowledge, he summons brāhmaṇas, friends and kings for auspicious coronation, rites, consecrated waters, Vedic chants and gifts. He takes forest-dwelling initiation; Paraśubāhu then rules.

evidence.paraphrase: Paraśubāhu rules by dharma and policy, gains three-world fame and wears a Mandāra-made Dhundhi image on his neck. He never worships without śamī and dūrvā. He enjoys many pleasures and wives according to the text’s dharmic description, begets sons and gives gifts. After ruling a thousand YEARS, he places a son in his position and goes to heaven, where he remains for many kalpas with Dhundhi’s form. No specific named wife or successor is supplied.

evidence.paraphrase: Vyāsa asks where Vināyaka’s world is. Brahmā says he taught Nārada, who taught Mudgala, who told the Kāśī king. Vināyaka created it with Kāmadāyinī Śakti and named it Nijaloka. The king saw it from a vehicle with bodily eyes; those arriving have no sorrow or duality. A Brāhma-kalpa residence/jyotirūpa clause precedes the Ikṣu-ocean experience and is left unnormalized. The indestructible seat survives dissolution and is the Lord’s eternal resting place. Siddhi/Buddhi serve, Sāmaveda sings, the wish-tree gives conceived desires and unimagined wealth appears. Brahmā admits inability to fully describe it.

narrative_events.details: Kīrti asks about simultaneous feet at Tuṇḍana and Kāśī; the sage answers by cosmic omnipresence, unlimited forms and divine will.
Divodāsa’s character, Brahmā kingdom grant and exclusion of gods; tapas/rain and righteous administration relieve drought. Wife’s naming remains under review.
Drought precedes Śiva’s visit to the ten-thousand-year ascetic; own form/realm granted. Gods inspect a faultless king and stay in Kāśī.
The kingdom’s duties, worship and crops remain faultless. Successive envoys cannot find or create a fault and settle in Kāśī.
Śiva asks a māyā strategy to reduce royal merit; Dhundhi promises, honors family/guru and adopts an astrologer disguise.
Thought/dream/palm knowledge and effective healing, progeny and three-day wealth grants win people’s attention.
Court women abandon household duties; king forgets his former deity. Astrologer declines material patronage and directs obedience to a visitor on the seventeenth day.
King vows obedience. Viṣṇu’s Bauddha and Kamalā roles draw people from ritual duties through source-attributed māyā teachings, producing wrong.
Visitor links royal merit to residence; four-armed revelations, reflection and recognition lead the king to refuge, liberation request and royal-seal surrender.
Viṣṇu reports the abandoned kingdom; Divodāsa gives up insignia, installs his liṅga and waits in tapas.
Dhundhi sends for Śiva; the bull-riding return favors the fasting sage and brings praise of cosmic functions and divine precedents.
Śiva asks continuing protection and states worship/name/hymn phalas, installs the Gaṇḍakī image and actually gives Divodāsa liberation. Sage closes the beneficial māyā account.
The sage departs. Mother and son go to the Kāśī festival, offer roadside leaves/flowers, remain fasting and receive the ten-armed vision and boon invitation.
After a hymn and revival recap, Kīrti asks her son’s devotion, fame, detached rule, long life, virtues, strength and victory.
All requests granted, with thousand-year life/thousand sacrifices, end-remembrance/form promise; own axe given and Parśubāhu name assigned.
Homecoming, parental embrace/report and coronation rites; father takes forest-dwelling initiation and son begins rule.
A thousand-year righteous reign, constant leaf worship, wives/sons and generosity; succession followed by heaven for many kalpas in Dhundhi’s form.
